question: In 1206 a Mongol chieftain named Temüjin was proclaimed supreme ruler of the steppe tribes. By what title is he known to history?
source_excerpt: until 1206, when he was bestowed the title of "Genghis Khan" (sometimes "Chinggis Khan"), which means "Universal Ruler"

extra.why_interesting: Most players know the title but not the birth name. Giving the birth name and the empire lets them reason their way to the famous title.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Temüjin was given the title Genghis (Chinggis) Khan by the 1206 quriltai; no later developments affect this.

explanation: Temüjin took the title Genghis Khan and went on to found what became the largest contiguous land empire in history.

question: Which Roman emperor, notorious for his erratic behaviour, was said to have planned to make his favourite horse a consul?
source_excerpt: According to legend, Caligula planned to make the horse a consul

extra.why_interesting: The absurdity of a horse as a senior magistrate is delightful. The emperor's reputation for madness gives players a clear path to the answer.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's Incitatus article says that, according to legend, Caligula planned to make his favourite horse a consul. The question is already hedged with 'was said to'.

explanation: According to Suetonius, the horse Incitatus had a marble stall, an ivory manger and servants of its own. Many historians think the consul plan was Caligula mocking the Senate.

question: In which year did Constantinople fall to the Ottoman Turks, bringing the Byzantine Empire to an end?
source_excerpt: The Fall of Constantinople on May 29, 1453, marked a significant turning point in history, leading to the end of the Byzantine Empire.

extra.why_interesting: Every distractor is a real turning point that players may confuse with the fall: the Crusader sack in 1204, the Battle of Kosovo in 1389 and Columbus in 1492.
extra.verification_notes: Constantinople fell on 29 May 1453, the conventional end of the Byzantine Empire; the other options are unrelated events (1204 Fourth Crusade, 1389 Kosovo, 1492 Columbus).

explanation: Sultan Mehmed II took the city in 1453, partly by dragging ships overland to get around the great chain that blocked the Golden Horn.

question: Determined to make his nobles look more Western European, which Russian tsar introduced a tax on men who kept their beards?
source_excerpt: In 1698, Tsar Peter I of Russia (also known as Peter the Great) introduced a beard tax after he developed anti-beard sentiments following a tour of Western Europe.

extra.why_interesting: Taxing facial hair sounds like a joke. Players who know which tsar wanted Russia to look European can reason their way to the answer.
extra.verification_notes: Peter I introduced Russia's beard tax in 1698 after his Western Europe tour; no competing tsar or newer development found (see Wikipedia Beard tax page).

explanation: Bearded men who paid were given a token stamped with the words 'the beard is a superfluous burden'. Peter also reportedly cut off some courtiers' beards himself.

question: Alexander the Great founded a city in present-day Pakistan named after his beloved warhorse. What was the horse called?
source_excerpt: The city was named after Alexander's beloved horse, Bucephalus, which died there.

extra.why_interesting: Naming a city after a pet is a lovely human detail about a conqueror. The name is famous enough that history fans will reach it, while others score a proud near-miss.
extra.verification_notes: Britannica confirms Bucephala in modern Pakistan was named after Alexander's horse Bucephalus.

explanation: According to legend, a young Alexander tamed Bucephalus by turning the horse to face the sun so it couldn't see its own shadow. The city of Bucephala was founded on the Hydaspes river after the horse died.

question: After touring Western Europe, Russia's Peter the Great put a tax on something many Russian men wore proudly. Those who paid had to carry a metal token as proof. What was taxed?
topic: Peter the Great and Imperial Russia
source_excerpt: Those who paid the tax were issued a token as proof of payment (the beard token).

extra.why_interesting: Players expect an emperor's tax to target land, salt or trade goods. The answer is a personal grooming choice, and the tax came with a physical token to carry. The 'proudly wore' and 'token' footholds let a thoughtful player reason toward something on the body, so it feels winnable and gives an 'of course!' moment.
extra.verification_notes: Peter the Great's beard tax, with copper/metal beard tokens as proof of payment, is well documented and no newer event changes it; the question says 'proudly', which is a loose but harmless description.

explanation: Peter saw beards as a symbol of old-fashioned Russia and wanted his court to look European. He reportedly shaved some nobles' beards off himself.
